page: Microsoft Azure D8pds_v5 is an ARM-based general-purpose virtual machine powered by an Ampere ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 processor operating at 3.0 GHz. The configuration provides 8 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs with a single thread per core, managed via the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. Memory capacity totals 32.0 GB of RAM, establishing a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory allocation of 4.0 GB per core. In addition to support for Azure Premium Storage, the hardware bundles 322 GB of local SSD storage for temporary data caching. The instance does not include a discrete GPU accelerator.

In synthetic and application-level benchmarks, the D8pds_v5 shows balanced multi-core efficiency, reaching a multi-core stress-ng score of 14512.61 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 5955.0. Memory subsystem testing yields 68.42 GB/sec for uncached 256 MB reads and 41.29 GB/sec for large block writes. However, single-core execution capacity is modest, scoring 1055.0 on single-core Geekbench and exhibiting weak metrics in single-threaded bzip3 decompression at 7.34 GB/sec. Hardware-level security features include cryptographic AES acceleration, while x86-specific instruction sets such as AVX-512 and AMX are not present on this ARM architecture.

The combination of dedicated non-hyperthreaded cores and balanced memory capacity provides stable concurrency for multi-threaded server tasks. The platform demonstrates solid performance in software compilation with Clang (9344.0), Redis operations (10.92 million operations per second), and static web delivery (8.73 GB/sec). These characteristics make the instance a solid fit for ARM-native continuous integration pipelines, web servers, in-memory caching layers, and containerized application microservices.

It integrates 32.0 GB of RAM, delivering a 1:4 core-to-memory ratio, alongside 322 GB of bundled local SSD storage. Benchmark results show steady multi-core execution, recording 14512.61 in multi-core stress-ng tests, 5955.0 in Geekbench multi-core, and 10.92 million operations per second in Redis SET operations. However, single-core processing is limited, with lower scores in single-threaded bzip3 decompression and Geekbench single-core evaluations. Hardware cryptographic acceleration is supported via ARM AES instructions, though x86 vector extensions are absent. This configuration provides solid resource density for cloud-native web serving, caching clusters, software compilation pipelines, and containerized microservices.
